title: How are lambda expressions implemented at the bytecode level (`invokedynamic` + a runtime-generated function object via `LambdaMetafactory`), and why is that cheaper than an anonymous-class instance per lambda?
shortTitle: How are lambda expressions implemented at the bytecode level?
keyPoints: A lambda compiles to a private synthetic method plus an invokedynamic site bootstrapped by LambdaMetafactory.
The first execution calls LambdaMetafactory, which creates the functional-interface implementation and caches it in the call site.
No separate class file is produced at compile time, so JARs are smaller and there are fewer classes to load and verify.
A non-capturing lambda is created once and reused as a singleton, allocating nothing after the first link.
A capturing lambda needs an instance holding the captured values, but it is still cheaper in class count than an anonymous class.
The JIT compiler can inline through lambda calls because the body is a method in the enclosing class.
The same invokedynamic plus bootstrap-method machinery powers string concatenation and record components.

s1_definition.oneliner: A lambda compiles to a private synthetic method plus an invokedynamic site bootstrapped by LambdaMetafactory, which lazily creates and caches the functional-interface implementation, avoiding a separate class file and repeated allocations per lambda.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Synthetic method** – the lambda body compiles to a `private static` (or instance) method in the enclosing class, not a separate class file.
- **invokedynamic** – a bytecode instruction that is unlinked when loaded and gets linked on first execution by calling a bootstrap method.
- **LambdaMetafactory** – the bootstrap method that creates the functional-interface implementation, typically by generating a small hidden class at run time.
- **CallSite caching** – the factory returns a `CallSite` whose target is cached, so subsequent executions reuse it with no re-bootstrapping.
- **Non-capturing singleton** – a lambda that captures no state is created once and reused, allocating nothing on hot paths.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India needs a small rule like "charge a fee only if the balance is above ten lakh." With the old anonymous-class approach, the bank would print a brand-new permanent rulebook for that one rule up front, a whole class file. The lambda approach is smarter: the bank writes the rule as a short private note in the existing manual and leaves a placeholder that says "ask the factory to wire this up the first time we actually need it." The first time a clerk reaches that spot, the factory assembles a tiny adapter pointing at the note and pins it there, so every later clerk reuses the same adapter.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Anonymous Class (Old Way):
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ Compiler         │
  │                  │
  │ MyClass.java     │──▶ MyClass.class
  │                  │──▶ MyClass$1.class  (anonymous class 1)
  │                  │──▶ MyClass$2.class  (anonymous class 2)
  │                  │──▶ MyClass$3.class  (anonymous class 3)
  └─────────────────┘    Each callback = new class file

  Lambda (New Way):
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ Compiler         │
  │                  │
  │ MyClass.java     │──▶ MyClass.class
  │                  │    (lambda bodies are methods inside)
  │                  │    (invokedynamic sites = placeholders)
  └─────────────────┘

  Runtime Bootstrap:
  ┌───────────┐  first call   ┌──────────────────┐
  │invokedyn  │──────────────▶│ LambdaMetafactory│
  │amic site  │               │                  │
  └───────────┘               │ 1. Read method   │
       │                      │    handle        │
       │                      │ 2. Generate tiny │
       │                      │    hidden class  │
       │                      │ 3. Return cached │
       │                      │    CallSite      │
       │                      └──────────────────┘
       │
       ▼ subsequent calls
  ┌───────────┐
  │ Cached    │  (no re-bootstrapping,
  │ CallSite  │   non-capturing = singleton)
  └───────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A lambda expression is not compiled into a separate anonymous class. Instead, the compiler emits the lambda body as a private synthetic method in the enclosing class, and at the use site it emits an invokedynamic bytecode instruction whose bootstrap method is LambdaMetafactory. The first time that invokedynamic site executes, the JVM calls LambdaMetafactory, which creates an object implementing the target functional interface whose single method forwards to the synthetic method, and then caches that linkage in the call site so every later execution reuses it with no re-bootstrapping.

This is cheaper than an anonymous class per lambda for four reasons. No separate class file is produced at compile time, so JARs are smaller and there are fewer classes to load. The creation strategy is decided at run time by LambdaMetafactory, so the JDK can optimize it. Most importantly, a non-capturing lambda is created once and reused as a singleton, so a hot loop allocates nothing after the first link. And the bootstrap cost is lazy, paid only the first time the site runs.

In the transaction processor at National Bank of India Rajesh used this heavily. The rules engine applies many small predicates and transformations as lambdas, which kept the class count down and, for non-capturing rules like a credit-check threshold, avoided per-iteration allocations in hot filter loops. A rule that closes over a run-time threshold needs an instance holding that value, while a stateless rule becomes a reused singleton.

Remember one sentence: a lambda compiles to a private method plus an invokedynamic site bootstrapped by LambdaMetafactory, which lazily creates and caches the functional-interface implementation so non-capturing lambdas are singletons and no extra class files are produced.
